t.church of achao@-42.5,-73.5:
Chiloé is an island of rain, green hills and wooden churches, off the coast of southern Chile, and the church of Achao, on the small island of Quinchao, is the oldest of them. Built in the eighteenth century by Jesuit missionaries and local carpenters, it is made entirely of wood, joined with wooden pegs instead of nails, and its interior is painted in soft blues and whites, with a vaulted ceiling and carved altars. It is one of the sixteen churches of Chiloé inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.

The Jesuits arrived in Chiloé in the seventeenth century and established a system of missions, travelling by boat between the islands to visit communities. The churches they inspired combine European architecture with local building traditions, using the abundant timber of the islands and the skills of boat builders. After the Jesuits were expelled in 1767, Franciscans continued the work, and the churches became the centres of island communities, each with its own patron saint and festival.

Getting to Achao is an adventure. From Castro or Dalcahue on the main island, you take a short ferry from Dalcahue to Quinchao, and then ride across the island to Achao, a small town on the eastern shore. The roads on Chiloé are a mix of paved highways and gravel tracks, winding over green hills with views of the sea and the snowy Andes on the mainland on clear days. Rain is frequent and can be heavy, so waterproof gear is essential. The wind can be strong, and the gravel roads can be muddy.

Achao has basic services, and fuel is available in Dalcahue and Castro, so fill up before crossing. The food in Chiloé is famous: curanto, a dish of shellfish, meat, potatoes and dumplings cooked in a pit in the ground, covered with leaves. Chiloé has hundreds of varieties of native potatoes. The Dalcahue Sunday market, with crafts and food, is lively. Standing inside the church of Achao, with rain drumming on the wooden roof and the smell of old timber all around, is a moving experience.
t.church of dalcahue@-42.4,-73.6:
Chiloé is a damp, green island off the coast of southern Chile, and its wooden churches are its soul. The Church of Dalcahue stands on the waterfront of a small town on the eastern side of the island, facing the inner sea and the islands of the archipelago, with a long arcaded porch along its front and a tall tower rising above. Built entirely of wood, with shingles cut from native trees, it is one of sixteen churches inscribed in 2000 as the Churches of Chiloé.

The churches reflect a meeting of cultures. Jesuit missionaries arrived in the seventeenth century and set up a circuit of missions around the islands, and later Franciscans continued the work. The local people, Indigenous Huilliche and mestizo islanders, built the churches using their skills as boat builders and carpenters, joining timbers with wooden pegs and covering walls in shingles. The result is a unique style, simple yet elegant, with vaulted ceilings that look like the inverted hull of a ship.

Dalcahue is famous for its Sunday market, where islanders sell woollen goods, wooden crafts, potatoes, seafood and baskets. The town also has palafitos, houses on stilts over the water, and a small ferry crosses to the island of Quinchao, where the church at Achao is one of the oldest in the group. Chiloé's cuisine is distinctive: curanto, a feast of shellfish, meat, potatoes and dumplings cooked in a pit with hot stones and covered with leaves, is the most famous dish, and there are many potato varieties grown only on the island.

Riding in Chiloé is not about speed. The main road, Ruta 5, runs down the island from the ferry at Chacao to Quellón in the south, while smaller roads lead to villages and churches, often unpaved and muddy. Rain is frequent all year, sometimes for days, and the wind can be strong. The landscape is lush and green, with rolling hills, forests and sea views. Summer, from December to February, is the driest season.

Dalcahue has fuel and basic services, and Castro, fifteen kilometres away, is the island's capital, with more shops, restaurants and accommodation. The ferry from the mainland at Pargua takes about half an hour. Bring good waterproofs.
Gobustan is a stony, wind-scoured landscape of low hills and mesas south of Baku, near the shores of the Caspian Sea, and on its rocks, people carved images over thousands of years: hunters with bows, boats with rowers, dancers, wild cattle, deer and goats. More than six thousand petroglyphs have been recorded here, dating back as far as the end of the last ice age, and the Gobustan Rock Art Cultural Landscape was listed by UNESCO in 2007. The coordinates fall near Jinghindagh mountain and Yazylytepe hill, two of the main areas of rock art, with the larger Boyukdash mountain nearby.

Walking among the boulders, with the Caspian shimmering in the distance and the wind whistling through the rocks, you find carvings on almost every surface, some faint, some sharp and clear. The boats are particularly intriguing, suggesting a long tradition of navigation on the Caspian. At the foot of Boyukdash, a Latin inscription left by a Roman legion, the Twelfth Fulminata, in the first century AD, is one of the easternmost Roman inscriptions ever found. The visitor centre at the site has a modern museum that explains the history and meaning of the carvings.

Nearby, the area is also famous for its mud volcanoes: small cones that bubble and burp grey mud, sometimes with flames from escaping gas. Azerbaijan has a large share of the world's mud volcanoes, and visiting them is a strange and memorable experience. The roads to them are unpaved and become impassable after rain.

For riders, the main approach is the highway south from Baku toward Salyan and the Iranian border, a busy, fast road along the coast, with oil and gas installations, industrial areas and the sea on one side. The landscape is arid and open, with strong winds, especially the cold northerly wind that sweeps across the Absheron peninsula. Summers are very hot, winters cool and windy; spring and autumn are the best times to visit.

Qobustan, about twelve kilometres away, and Sangachal have fuel and basic services; Baku, an hour's ride to the north, has everything. Try a plate of plov, the Azerbaijani rice dish, which comes in dozens of varieties, or kebabs with fresh herbs and flatbread, and drink a glass of strong black tea, often served with jam. Back in Baku, the walled old city, with its Maiden Tower and Palace of the Shirvanshahs, makes a good end to the day.
t.walled city of baku with the shirvanshah:
Baku is windy by name and by nature, and the old walled city on the Caspian shore has been catching the wind for about a thousand years. Inside the walls, known locally as Icherisheher, a maze of narrow stone lanes winds between mosques, caravanserais and houses with carved balconies. The Maiden Tower, a stout round tower of mysterious age and purpose, rises near the sea, and the Palace of the Shirvanshahs, built in the fifteenth century as the residence of the rulers of Shirvan, sits on the hill above. UNESCO listed the walled city and the palace together in 2000.

Baku's story is also a story of oil. The Apsheron peninsula, on which the city stands, has natural seeps of oil and gas, and fire has been part of its religious and cultural history for centuries; later, in the nineteenth century, oil made fortunes, and the grand buildings of the boom period stand just outside the old city walls. The Nobel brothers, among others, built fortunes here, and the modern skyline of glass towers and the Flame Towers, lit at night, are a continuation of that wealth.

Riding here is an urban experience. Traffic in central Baku is dense and fast, with confident, sometimes aggressive drivers, so ride defensively and anticipate sudden lane changes. The old city is largely pedestrian, with steep cobbled streets that are unsuitable for a loaded bike, so park outside the walls and explore on foot. Beyond the city, the coast road along the Caspian is a pleasant run, and the highway south toward Gobustan crosses a dry, tawny landscape of low hills and mud volcanoes. The wind can be strong on exposed stretches, and summers are very hot, so spring and autumn are the best seasons.

Fuel is easy to find on the main roads around Baku, with Badamdar and other suburbs offering several stations. Food in the old city includes plov, kebabs, dolma and rich dishes flavoured with saffron, served with strong black tea in small glasses, and the cafés in the courtyards are good places to rest in the shade. Plan at least a couple of hours for the walled city, preferably early morning when the light is soft and the lanes are quiet.
t.churgh of caguach@-42.5,-73.3:
Chiloé is a green, rainy island off the coast of southern Chile, and its wooden churches are among the most remarkable buildings in South America. Jesuit missionaries began building them in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and after the Jesuits were expelled, local carpenters, used to building boats, carried on the work with larch, cypress and native timber, producing churches with shingled towers, porches and curved wooden ceilings like upturned hulls. UNESCO listed a group of sixteen of them in 2000, and the church on Caguach island is a famous one, linked to the pilgrimage of Jesús Nazareno that draws devotees each year at the end of August.

Caguach is a small island in the Quinchao group, reached by boat, and the church stands at the centre of a close, quiet community. A motorcycle will not take you there directly, so the realistic plan is to leave the bike on the main island, take a ferry or local boat as far as it goes, and walk the rest. Dalcahue, about thirty-five kilometres away on the mainland of Chiloé, has its own famous wooden church, a busy crafts market, and the harbour from which boats leave for the smaller islands.

Riding on Chiloé is a joy. The island is reached by a short ferry across the Chacao channel, and the main road, Route 5, runs south through rolling green country with sheep, small farms, and glimpses of fjords and bays. Side roads to Dalcahue and Castro are paved but narrow, with bends, short climbs and plenty of rain. The weather is changeable, with showers and wind in any season, so waterproofs are essential, and summer, from December to March, is the driest and most pleasant time. Mist across the water and the smell of woodsmoke give the island its particular atmosphere.

Dalcahue has fuel, small restaurants and shops, and you should fill up there or in Castro before heading anywhere remote. Try curanto, a traditional dish of shellfish, meat and potatoes cooked in a pit with hot stones, or a bowl of seafood stew, and buy knitted woollens at the market. Ferry timetables depend on tides and weather, so check locally and allow a buffer in your schedule, because the sea sets the pace here.
t.church of castro@-42.5,-73.8:
Castro's church is the first thing that makes visitors to Chiloé stop talking. San Francisco stands on the Plaza de Armas of the island's capital, a big building with a corrugated-metal skin painted in yellow and violet, two towers and a wooden interior that is mostly hand-cut native timber. It was built in the early twentieth century to replace an earlier church that burned, by an Italian architect, and it is one of the sixteen Chiloé churches that UNESCO listed in 2000. The rest are mostly smaller and older, scattered along the coast, built by Jesuit missionaries and their Chilote carpenters, who were boat builders first and used what they knew. If you tip your head back inside, the vaulted ceiling looks like an upturned hull.

Getting here is half the fun. The Panamericana, Route 5, comes south across the Chacao Channel by ferry, and the crossing takes about half an hour with dolphins sometimes alongside. From the ferry the road runs down the island through rolling green hills, pasture and small farms, with the odd flash of sea. It is open, windy and frequently wet, so pack proper waterproofs and expect gravel-edge surprises on some secondary roads. Chiloé's rain feels cooler and softer than it looks on the forecast, and the light afterwards, with steam off the tarmac and silver channels beyond the hedges, is why you carry a camera.

Castro itself is a proper town of around thirty thousand, with fuel stations, workshops, supermarkets and plenty of cafes. The old stilt houses, the palafitos, line the waterfront at the edge of the town, painted in bright colours and raised on poles above the tidal water. Look at them near high tide, when the sea is under the floorboards. For lunch, ask for curanto, the island's dish of shellfish, meat and potato cooked in a pit or a pot, a meal built for people who spent the day in cold weather.

Dalcahue and Chonchi, both a short ride away, have their own churches and markets, and you can easily spend a day looping between them. Put petrol in Castro in any case, since the southern part of the island thins out quickly. Keep an eye on the weather and give the church a proper half hour, and you will see why the island's carpenters are still famous.
t.church of ichuac@-42.6,-73.7:
Chiloe is a large, green, rainy island off the coast of southern Chile, and its wooden churches are among the most unusual in the Americas. In the seventeenth century, Jesuit missionaries arrived to convert the Chono and Huilliche people, and they found a population of skilled carpenters and boatbuilders. The churches that arose from this meeting, built entirely of local timber, with shingles of alerce cypress and pegs instead of nails, combine European plans with the techniques of ship carpentry. About sixteen of them were listed by UNESCO in 2000, and the one at Ichuac is among the most appealing, on the island of Lemuy, a short ferry ride from the main island.

Lemuy is a small, hilly, quiet island, reached by a ferry from Puchilco, near Chonchi, that takes a few minutes. The roads are narrow and mostly gravel, winding between small farms, hedges, sheep and woodland, with views of the channels and the white peaks of the mainland Andes beyond. The churches stand on the shore or on a rise, painted in colours of white, yellow, blue and red, and the interiors have wooden vaulted ceilings that look like the inside of an upturned boat. If a church is closed, ask in the nearest house, because someone usually has the key. The other labels, Detif and Caguach, are on other small islands and show how many churches are scattered across the archipelago.

The ride is not about speed. The roads are rough and sometimes muddy, the rain is frequent, and the weather can turn from sunshine to squall in minutes, so waterproof gear is essential. The gravel can be loose, and animals wander freely. The best months are from December to March, when the days are long and relatively dry, though a downpour is never far away. In winter, the island is wet, dark and very quiet.

Look for the fishermen's stalls selling fresh seafood, and the local dish curanto, a stew of shellfish, meat and potatoes cooked in a hole in the ground. Chiloe is known for hundreds of varieties of potato, and you can taste several of them in a single meal.
t.church of chonchi@-42.6,-73.8:
Chonchi is a small port town on the east coast of Chiloe, built on a steep hillside above the channel, and locals sometimes call it the city of three floors, because its streets climb in terraces from the waterfront to the plaza and the church above. The church of San Carlos de Borromeo, painted in warm yellow and red and crowned with a tall tower, was built in the nineteenth century, in the typical style of the island, and it dominates the square. Inside, it has the characteristic wooden columns and a ceiling like the hull of a ship, and the interior smells of old timber and wax.

It forms part of the UNESCO group of the Churches of Chiloe, and gives a good sense of how important these buildings were to the community. For centuries, the missionaries visited the scattered villages by boat, and the local people, organised in lay groups, kept the churches going, maintained them and held the festivals of the saints. The tradition of the minga, in which a whole community moves a house or a building across the land, using oxen and logs, is still remembered here. Chonchi was also a centre of the Chilote timber trade, and the old houses on the main street, covered with wooden shingles, are charming.

Chonchi is a good base for riding. The main road on Chiloe, Route 5, is the southern end of the Pan-American Highway, and runs from the ferry at Chacao in the north through Ancud and Castro down to Quellon, with a smooth surface and views of the sea, hills and farms. Side roads lead to little fishing villages, with stilt houses called palafitos and quiet beaches, and are mostly gravel. The ferry from Chonchi to Lemuy leaves from nearby. Weather is the main issue, with frequent rain and wind, and even the best summer days can turn grey and wet.

Fuel is available in Chonchi, and Castro, the capital of the island, seventeen kilometres to the north, has larger supermarkets, hotels and restaurants. Try the local seafood, such as mussels, clams and salmon, and the milcao, a potato bread, and warm yourself with a strong cup of tea or coffee. Respect the churches as places of worship, dress simply, and ask before taking photographs inside.
t.church of vilupulli@-42.6,-73.8:
On the island of Chiloé, in southern Chile, the churches are made of wood, and the whole archipelago has been built around that fact. Vilupulli is one of the sixteen churches that UNESCO lists as an exceptional example of a local tradition, combining European ideas with the shipbuilding skills of Chilote carpenters. Jesuit missionaries arrived in the seventeenth century and planned a circuit of chapels, and after they were expelled the communities kept them going, with local families caring for the buildings and holding festivals. The result is a string of timber churches with plank walls, shingled towers and painted interiors, each in a fishing village or on a quiet inlet.

The church stands close to Chonchi, a town of about 12,000 people on the eastern coast of the main island, known for its steep streets and its wooden houses. The surrounding country is green and damp: small farms, hedgerows, patches of native forest and the grey Pacific light. Expect rain, even in summer, and wind off the sea. Weather changes within an hour, and the roads are slick, so keep your speed down and watch for livestock.

Chiloé is reached by ferry across the Chacao Channel from the mainland, and the Panamericana, Route 5, runs down the island's spine. It is a pleasant, rolling road with moderate traffic, a decent surface and glimpses of the sea. Side roads to the churches are narrower and sometimes gravel, so check conditions. Fuel is available in Chonchi and Castro, the island's capital with about 30,000 people, and the smaller villages may not have any, so top up in town.

Food is part of the pleasure. Curanto, a stew of shellfish, meat and potatoes traditionally cooked in a pit with hot stones, is the island's best-known dish, and you will also find fresh salmon, mussels and the large variety of native potatoes that Chiloé is proud of. The islanders have a rich folklore, with tales of sea spirits and ghost ships, and the churches take part in a festive tradition of boats and processions. Take a moment inside if the church is open, where the wooden ceiling often looks like the hull of an upturned boat, and a sense of the craftsmanship becomes clear.
t.church of chelin@-42.6,-73.5:
Getting to Chelín is part of the pleasure, because it lies on Lemuy, a small island off Chiloé's east coast reached by a short ferry. From Chonchi the crossing is quick, and the vehicles line up on a ramp, with the sea bright and often choppy. Lemuy is a rolling island of small farms, potato fields, sheep and hedged lanes, with a population that is mostly spread over small settlements. There are no big towns here at all, and fuel is not something to count on, so fill up in Chonchi, about 21 km away by the map, before you cross.

The church at Chelín belongs to the same UNESCO group as its neighbours on Lemuy, including Detif, Aldachildo and Ichuac. These are small wooden buildings that came out of the Jesuit mission system and the local boat-building tradition, with walls of planks and roofs and towers covered in wooden shingles called tejuelas. Chilote carpenters used what the forest gave them, mostly alerce and cypress, and their joints are pegged and fitted rather than nailed. The church at Chelín sits by the water, and the setting, with fishing boats pulled up and a grey sea beyond, is as much part of it as the building.

The riding on the island is slow and rewarding. Roads are a mixture of paved and gravel, narrow and hilly, with views over the channels and the mainland Andes when the cloud lifts. The best months are December to March, when days are long and the temperature is mild, but be ready for rain at any time of year. After rain the gravel is slippery and the potholes fill with water. Keep an eye on livestock, since cows and sheep treat the road as a pasture.

Food on Lemuy is plain and fresh: shellfish, bread baked in village kitchens and dishes made with the island's potatoes. Chiloé is thought to be the home of many of the potato varieties found around the world, and farmers still grow dozens of types. Time your trip around the ferry timetable, which can change, and take a coat. The sense of distance from the mainland is part of what makes it worthwhile, and a long still afternoon beside the church, with the light on the water, is memorable.
t.church of aldachildo@-42.6,-73.6:
Aldachildo is another of the small wooden churches on Lemuy, and it asks you to think about how the Chilote churches were actually used. They were not built for tourists, or even mainly for Sundays. When Jesuit missionaries began to organise the islands in the seventeenth century, they did not have enough priests to be everywhere. So they trained local laymen to look after chapels, lead prayers and baptise, and the missionaries themselves sailed round the circuit once a year, on a kind of pilgrimage that the communities still remember with an annual festival. After the Jesuits were expelled in the eighteenth century, those lay guardians kept the system alive.

The result is a landscape of chapels placed where people lived: on a headland, by a beach, at the edge of a hamlet. Aldachildo's church fits this pattern, in a settlement of farms and fishing, on an island of rolling pasture and wind-bent trees. The nearest large town is Chonchi, about 14 km away across the water, and Castro, the provincial capital, is a bit farther off. Lemuy has little in the way of shops and services, so bring cash, snacks and fuel.

The ride to the church is the kind that suits patience. Gravel sections wind between fences and stone walls, and the road rises and falls in short bursts, with views down toward calm bays where oyster and mussel farms float in rows. In rain the surface turns to mud, and the wind can come in hard from the Pacific side. If the sky is clear, you can see volcanoes on the mainland across the Gulf of Corcovado, snowy cones far to the east.

Take the time to look closely if the doors are open. The interior is usually painted in soft blues and whites, with a ceiling shaped like a ship's hull, and the wooden saints show decades of patient repair. The whole island culture revolves around the minga, a communal work party, and once even whole houses were dragged across the water on floats by teams of oxen and neighbours. The church stands as a record of that cooperative habit, and it is worth leaving a small donation if there is a box.
t.boyukdash mountain@40.1,49.4:
Gobustan is a rocky, windswept plateau about sixty kilometres south of Baku, where outcrops of limestone and sandstone rise out of a plain of dry grass, and the Caspian Sea glints on the horizon. Boyukdash, the Big Rock, is one of the boulders that make up this open-air gallery, and its sides are covered with carvings called petroglyphs made by people who lived and hunted here over thousands of years, some of them tens of thousands. UNESCO listed the area in 2007.

The images are vivid and direct: bulls, deer, horses and goats, hunters with bows, dancing figures and lines of boats with rowers. The sea level of the Caspian has changed many times, so the shore that these people knew is now far away. The Norwegian explorer Thor Heyerdahl visited in the 1960s and found that the boat carvings resembled the reed ships he knew, and he used that to support a theory of ancient links between the Caspian and Scandinavia, a theory that scholars have not widely accepted. Near the main site is Gaval Dash, a stone that rings like a drum when struck.

The landscape has another peculiarity. Nearby are mud volcanoes, small cones that bubble with grey mud and gas, among the most active in the world, and the road passes areas of strange, moonlike terrain. The ride from Baku follows a fast, modern highway south along the coast, with oil pumps nodding in the fields, and then turns inland. Wind is a constant, strong enough to push a bike, and summers are very hot with dust. Spring and autumn are better, when the plateau is green or golden.

Qobustan town, a few kilometres away, has fuel and simple cafes, and Baku offers every service you might want. Carry water, sun protection and a camera. A modern museum at the entrance shows the history, and guides explain the carvings in English. Try a cup of black tea with sweet pastries, such as pakhlava, after the walk, and allow a couple of hours for the site.
t.puerto montt@-41.5,-72.9:
Puerto Montt is where the Carretera Austral starts, though few people would call it a pretty town. It is a busy port and salmon-farming centre on the Reloncaví Sound, with a grey waterfront, fish stalls and a rain record to match, and it was founded in 1853 by German colonists brought in under the direction of Vicente Pérez Rosales. Across the water, if the clouds allow, the cone of Osorno volcano shows up white against the sky, and the lakeside towns to the north, Puerto Varas and Frutillar, still show their Bavarian-style wooden houses.

The harbourside quarter of Angelmó is the place to go before leaving. Stalls and tiny restaurants sell smoked mussels, fresh shellfish and woollen goods, and you can try curanto, a southern Chilean dish of shellfish, meat and potatoes traditionally steamed in a pit. From the jetties, ferries leave for the islands and the long fjords of the south, a reminder that for much of Chilean Patagonia the sea was the only road until the highway was built.

Heading out, the Carretera Austral, Ruta 7, begins as an ordinary paved road, passing farmland and forest to the ferry at La Arena, which crosses to Puelche. Further south, a second ferry connects Hornopirén to Caleta Gonzalo, running through fjords and mountains. Ferry timetables are tight and reservations may be needed in summer, so check before you commit. Rain is frequent all year, and the great temperate rainforest depends on it. The driest and warmest months are January and February. Pack full waterproofs, because showers can come suddenly even then.

Puerto Montt is a big city of over a hundred and fifty thousand people, with fuel stations, motorcycle dealers, supermarkets and good hotels, so it is the place to sort out spares, tyres and supplies. Puerto Varas, seventeen kilometres away, is a more relaxed base. Fill up and buy extra snacks and water before the ferries, and keep cash handy for ticket offices, which do not always take cards.
t.cultural landscape of khinalig people an:
The Greater Caucasus in Azerbaijan is a wall of limestone and shale that rises abruptly from the Caspian lowlands, and at its heart lives one of the oldest and most isolated communities in the country. The Khinalig people speak a language found nowhere else, farm and herd at over two thousand metres, and live in stone houses with flat roofs that sit so close together that you can walk from one yard to the next across the rooftops. The village is among the highest permanently inhabited places in Europe, and in winter the snow can cut it off for days.

The pin on this map sits lower, in the foothills near Altıağac and Shamakhi, and it is better understood as the gateway to that high country than as the village itself. Shamakhi is an ancient town, once the capital of the Shirvan khans and a famous centre of silk and wine, and it keeps a large Friday mosque, an observatory on a nearby hill with a good view of the night sky, and a hillside of old domed tombs. The road toward the mountains leaves the plain in gentle curves and then climbs into wooded valleys where the air changes, the temperature drops and the smell of pine and woodsmoke takes over.

Riding conditions change quickly with altitude. Lower roads are paved and generally fine, with the odd pothole and a lot of sheep, while upper roads can be steep, narrow and patched, with long drops at the edge and no barrier worth the name. The weather is a serious factor. Mist, rain and sudden storms are common, even in summer, and from late autumn the high road can be snow-covered or icy. Late May to early October is the usual window. Early morning gives the clearest views of the high peaks, including Shahdag and Bazarduzu, the latter sitting above four thousand metres on the border with Russia.

Fuel and food are best taken in Shamakhi, a town of about thirty thousand people twenty-two kilometres away, since the hamlets in the hills have little more than basic shops and tea. In the villages, bread, cheese, honey and strong black tea are served with a hospitality that can make you late for the next stop. Carry a warm layer, enough water, and a map that works offline, because mobile signal disappears in the valleys.
t.baku@40.4,49.9:
Baku is a city of wind. The name is often said to come from a Persian phrase meaning a place battered by winds, and anybody who has stood on the Caspian boulevard on a bad day will believe it. The city curves around a bay on the western shore of the sea, with a medieval walled core, Icherisheher, rising behind the seafront, and the modern glass of the Flame Towers high above, lit by moving flames in the evening that can be seen from far across the water.

The old city is the place to start. Its narrow stone lanes hold the Shirvanshahs' Palace, a fifteenth-century complex of pale limestone, and the Maiden Tower, a stout round tower of unclear origin and many legends. The oil story is the other great layer. At the end of the nineteenth century this was one of the main oil-producing places in the world, and the Nobel brothers of Sweden built a fortune here. The grand mansions in the centre were built by oil barons of that age, and today's skyline is the product of a second oil boom. Outside the city, on the Absheron peninsula, you find the Fire Temple at Surakhani, built where natural gas once burned from the ground, and the strange mud volcanoes of Gobustan to the south, which bubble and gurgle.

For riders, Baku itself is a test of nerve. Traffic is fast and dense, lane discipline is a loose idea, and the cheerful honk is the universal language. Once you clear the outer districts, the open roads of the Absheron and the highway west toward Shamakhi and the Caucasus are easier. The ride to Khinalig takes several hours, starting with a long motorway section and finishing on mountain roads that need care. Weather is hot in summer, mild in spring and autumn, and winter brings cold winds off the sea.

Fuel is plentiful and cheap, with stations on every main road, and the city has a good café culture where you can order strong tea in a glass with sugar cubes and jam. The best season is spring and early autumn. The Caspian is brackish, shallow and not especially inviting for swimming near the city, but the sunsets are fine, the promenade is busy in the evenings, and the sound of the wind never really stops.
t.chaiten@-42.9,-72.7:
Chaitén is a town that was almost removed from the map. In May 2008 the volcano of the same name, which nobody had thought to be dangerous, erupted without warning after thousands of years asleep. Ash covered the whole region, the Río Blanco burst its banks and carved a new channel straight through the middle of the town, and the government ordered a complete evacuation. For a while there were plans to abandon the place and build a new capital elsewhere. Many people returned anyway, and today Chaitén has a few thousand people, rebuilt streets, and a lingering sense of resilience. On the hills above, the volcano still steams, and you can see the grey scar of the lava dome from the road.

For motorcyclists, Chaitén is a pivotal point on the Carretera Austral. It is where the ferries from Puerto Montt dock, which is how many riders arrive, and it marks the beginning of the long, wild run south toward Coyhaique. Buy fuel in town, since the next pumps are a long way off, and sort out your supplies, because after here villages become small and sparse. t.puerto varas@-41.3,-73.0:

t.makhachkala@43.0,47.5:

t.lago falkner@-40.5,-71.5:

t.lake sevan@40.6,45.0:

t.sulak canyon@43.0,46.8:

t.gimri viewpoint@42.7,46.8:

t.samur forest@41.8,48.6:

t.kezenoy am@42.8,46.2:

t.puyuhuapi@-44.3,-72.6:

t.kichikdash mountain@40.1,49.4:

Archaeologists believe the sea was close to the rocks in prehistoric times, and the boats fit that picture.

t.dalcahue@-42.4,-73.6:

t.osorno volcano@-41.1,-72.5:

t.antsirabe@-19.9,47.0:
Antsirabe sits at about fifteen hundred metres in the central highlands of Madagascar, and the altitude gives it a cool, dry climate that surprises visitors who expect the island to be tropical. t.ancud@-41.9,-73.8:
Ancud is the northern door to Chiloé, an island of rain, mist and wooden churches off the coast of southern Chile. t.castro@-42.5,-73.8:

t.frutillar@-41.1,-73.0:

t.petrohue falls@-41.1,-72.4:

t.ensenada@-41.2,-72.5:

t.hornopiren ferry@-42.0,-72.5:

t.futaleufu river roads@-43.2,-71.9:

t.gunib@42.4,47.0:

t.san martin de los andes@-40.2,-71.4:
San Martín de los Andes lies at the eastern end of Lake Lácar, in a pocket of Patagonian forest, and the town itself feels as though it were assembled from the surrounding trees: steep-roofed wooden chalets, carved signs, the smell of woodsmoke in the cooler months. t.derbent@42.1,48.3:

Roadside stalls sell fruit and fresh fish, and the sea is warm in late summer.

t.bariloche@-41.1,-71.3:
Bariloche stands on the southern shore of Lake Nahuel Huapi, in the Argentine Andes, and the place has the look of an alpine resort that has been picked up and set in Patagonia. t.esquel@-42.9,-71.3:

The park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the oldest trees are among the longest-lived on earth. Cruises on the lakes reach groves of ancient trunks. Ruta 40 passes through Esquel, a long run of open country with great sky and big distances between fuel stops, so fill your tank whenever you can. Esquel itself has several stations, supermarkets and mechanics. Wind can be fierce on the steppe, especially in the afternoon. The best season is from November to March, though nights stay cold.
t.antananarivo@-18.9,47.5:
Antananarivo, which everyone calls Tana, is built on a long ridge and a dozen hills in the middle of Madagascar's highlands, at about twelve hundred and eighty metres, and it looks like a city from another century. Red-brick houses with steep roofs and narrow balconies climb the slopes in terraces, rice paddies fill the valleys right up to the edge of town, and on the highest hill stands the Rova, the old royal palace, whose granite walls were rebuilt after a fire in 1995. In the morning, the city is wrapped in smoke from charcoal stoves and the air is cool, and in the afternoon, a warm light picks out the colours of the old houses.

Tana's story is that of the Merina kingdom, whose kings unified much of the island in the nineteenth century, helped by British advisers, before the French took over in 1896. The city has a lively, chaotic feel, with crowds on the streets, taxis that are small old Renault and Citroen cars, stalls selling everything from sunglasses to live chickens, and the sweet smell of frying doughnuts. Lake Anosy in the centre is ringed by jacaranda trees that bloom lilac in October. For food, try romazava, a beef and leaf stew, and zebu steaks with rice.

Madagascar drives on the right.

Carry water, a basic tool kit and spare tubes, and allow far more time than the map suggests. The dry season from May to October is the best time, with cool nights in the highlands.
t.gamsutl@42.3,47.0:
Gamsutl is a ghost village on a ridge in the mountains of central Dagestan, a cluster of stone houses clinging to a steep spur above a deep canyon, and it is one of the most photographed sights in the republic. The pin sits near the Gunib plateau, with Gunib itself about ten kilometres away, Tsurib and Kumukh a little further, and the nearest larger town, Khadzhalmakhi, close to twenty kilometres off.

Getting there is half the point. The mountain roads of Dagestan are narrow, steep and often cut straight across rock faces, with hairpins that tighten without warning and long drops on the outside. The surface varies between good tarmac and rough patches, and in places the final approach becomes a track. A road like this rewards patience: ride slowly, keep your line, and expect livestock and oncoming cars on blind corners. Early morning is cleaner and cooler, and the light on the canyon walls is wonderful. Avoid riding in or after heavy rain, because the rock is crumbly.

Gamsutl itself is a place of silence. It was once a thriving village of the Avar people, built in tiers on the mountainside, and for generations its inhabitants farmed, herded and traded from this eagle's nest. The last families left in the twentieth century, and the stone houses are now mostly empty, with doorways open to the wind. Standing among them you can feel how hard life was, and how clever the building was: houses stacked like steps, roofs doubling as neighbours' yards.

The landscape is astonishing. Gunib, famous for the final surrender of the imam Shamil to the Russian army in 1859 after his long resistance in the Caucasus wars, sits just along the plateau, and the whole area is layered with that history. The canyon below Gamsutl is cut in limestone and glows orange in late light. Eagles and griffon vultures ride the updrafts, and in spring the slopes are green with grass and scrub.

Take water and food, since there is nothing at the top, and tell someone where you are headed. Phone signal is patchy, and the roads are slow. Respect the place, because locals still consider the old village a heritage site.
t.chokh@42.3,47.0:
Chokh is another of Dagestan's mountain villages, one of those places where the whole settlement is a stack of stone houses on a hillside, with slate roofs, narrow lanes and a mosque and tower at the top. It lies in the same highland country as Gunib, about ten kilometres away, with Khadzhalmakhi, the nearest larger town, a little further off. Fuel and proper shops are down in the valleys, not here, so ride with a full tank and a bit of reserve.

The road is slow and the scenery is the point. Climbing from the Gunib plateau, you wind along ridgelines and through deep gorges, with views opening across layers of grey and green mountains that stretch toward the horizon. Corners are tight, narrow and often blind, and you share the tarmac with sheep, cattle, trucks and locals who drive these roads fast and confidently. The surface is patchy, so keep your speed under your sight line, and avoid the road after heavy rain. Spring brings green slopes and waterfalls, summer is hot below and clear on the ridges, and autumn is dry and golden.

Dagestani villages tend to specialise: some are famous for silver, others for carpets or pottery, and this highland country has a long habit of craft passed from one generation to the next. Chokh is known above all as a place to see an old stone village largely intact, with the traditional houses of the upper quarter still standing. Walking its lanes you can hear the village before you see it, with the sound of animals, water and conversation filtering between walls.

The surroundings are rugged and dry, with limestone cliffs, scrub oak and juniper, and terraces carved into the slopes by centuries of farmers. The mountains of Dagestan rank among the most culturally diverse places in the world, with dozens of languages spoken across tiny valleys, and the contrast between neighbouring villages can be striking. The Avar, Dargin and Lak peoples all live in this highland belt.

A ride here is best done with a guide or at least local advice. Take water, snacks, warm layers and a map saved offline. Sunset light on the stone is memorable, but do not be caught on the road after dark. The hospitality is warm, and a cup of tea is an easy offer to accept.
t.grozny@43.3,45.7:
Few cities have been rebuilt as completely as Grozny. The capital of Chechnya was flattened in the wars of the 1990s, and what you ride into now, with a population of well over two hundred thousand, is a city of wide boulevards, glass towers and carefully restored squares, built almost from scratch in the years since. Staraya Sunzha lies just to the northwest, and the Sunzha river, the city's namesake stream, runs through the middle.

It is a city stop, and a good one for supplies. Fuel is on every main road, food comes in generous portions, and the traffic is brisk but orderly. Come in from the north across the flat Terek plain and you notice how quickly the horizon changes: low fields, then the long blue line of the Caucasus to the south, which is where you are heading on the ride toward Kezenoy-Am. The city streets are wide and well surfaced, and the best time to move through is early, before the daytime traffic gets going.

Grozny began in 1818 as a Russian fortress, built under General Yermolov during the long Caucasian war, and the name means terrible or formidable. The city grew into an oil centre in the late nineteenth century, and the petroleum industry shaped it for generations. The most visible landmark now is the Akhmad Kadyrov mosque, a big white building with tall minarets that was among the largest in Europe when it opened, and it is lit at night, which gives the city a very distinct skyline. Next to it, the tall towers of the Grozny City complex rise above the river.

Chechen hospitality is a real thing, and you will notice it in a cafe: tea, flatbread, dumplings called zhizhig-galnash and plenty of conversation. Dress modestly in religious areas, be polite and respect local customs, and you will find people helpful. Check travel advisories for the region before you set out, because conditions and rules can change.

The ride south toward the mountains climbs along river valleys into steep forested country, and the contrast with the plain is striking. Fill the tank here, carry water and warm layers, and expect cooler, wetter conditions as you gain height.
t.la junta chile@-44.0,-72.4:
La Junta is a small town where two rivers meet, which is exactly what the name says, and it marks the point where the Carretera Austral leaves the Palena valley and its wet green forests and enters the northern edge of the Aysen region. About twelve hundred people live here, scattered along wide, quiet streets, with lakes close by and snow-capped peaks showing above the trees. It is a handy place on a very empty road, with a fuel pump, a few shops, simple restaurants and guesthouses.

The ride from Chaiten is one of the most beautiful stretches of the Carretera Austral. The road follows rivers and lakes through a thick, damp forest of southern beech, tree ferns and bamboo thickets, with waterfalls pouring down the hillsides and clouds hanging low on the mountains. The surface alternates between paved sections and gravel, with potholes, loose stones and wet corners, so a steady pace is wiser than a fast one. It rains here far more often than not, even in summer, and temperatures are cool, so waterproofs are essential. The best months are December to March, when the days are long and there is some chance of sunshine.

The Carretera Austral is the product of a determined national project. In the 1970s and 1980s, the Chilean government pushed a road through some of the most remote and rugged terrain in the country, mainly to link isolated settlements to the rest of Chile, and soldiers and engineers worked for years with explosives and heavy machinery. Before it, many communities could be reached only by boat or on horseback. The settlers of this area came in the twentieth century, clearing forest for cattle, and fires set to open pasture left scars that are still visible on some slopes.

The surrounding country is a temperate rainforest of enormous richness. Lakes Rosselot and Verde lie nearby, glacial rivers run turquoise, and the mountains are draped in ancient forest. Birds are everywhere, including the colourful chucao, a small bird that calls from the undergrowth, and rare mammals such as the pudu, a tiny deer, live in the forest.

Fill the tank here, since fuel stops are scarce on the road, and check the next stretch's conditions. Pack rain gear, spare parts and snacks, and enjoy the sense of remoteness.
t.queulat@-44.5,-72.5:
Queulat is one of the great set pieces of the Carretera Austral, a national park where a glacier hangs from a high ridge and spills a waterfall from its edge, and where the road climbs and twists through deep forest on the way to Puyuhuapi and the south. The park lies on the Pacific side of the Andes, in the rainy zone, and the nearest settlement of any size is Puerto Cisnes on the coast, with Puyuhuapi a little north on the fjord. Fuel is available in Puyuhuapi and along the main road, but not in the park.

The ride through the area is demanding and wonderful. The road climbs a steep, zig-zagging section with gravel, loose rock and narrow bends, and in places it is cut into the side of the valley with the forest rising above and falling away below. Rain is the rule, and when it comes the surface becomes slick and muddy, with waterfalls cutting across the road. Late spring to early autumn gives the safest conditions, and early morning offers the quietest road. The air is damp and cool, smelling of moss and rotting leaves, and the cloud often hangs low over the ridges.

The Carretera Austral itself is a marvel of stubborn engineering. It was built in the late twentieth century to link isolated parts of Chilean Patagonia, and the work here, through steep, wet, forested terrain, was among the most difficult. At the heart of the park, the Ventisquero Colgante, or hanging glacier, tumbles from a high ice field, feeding a milky lake, and a short trail leads to a viewpoint. The water is a startling blue-green, and the roar of the falls fills the valley.

Fill up in Puyuhuapi, carry spare clothes and tools, and give yourself time to stop. The sights here deserve patience.
t.petrohue@-41.1,-72.4:
Petrohue sits at the western end of Lake Todos los Santos, a deep green lake in the shadow of Osorno volcano, and the small settlement is the end of the road for anyone driving up from Puerto Varas. From Puerto Varas the road runs along the edge of Lake Llanquihue, with long, easy bends, views across the water to the volcano and the sweet smell of cut grass and pine. Past La Ensenada the road climbs into forest, passes lava fields and winds along the Petrohue River to the lake. The surface is good, the corners are gentle, and the main hazard is slow traffic of tour buses and cars at weekends. Early morning is best, and summer and early autumn bring the most reliable weather, though rain can arrive from the Pacific in any month.

The valley was settled by German immigrants in the nineteenth century, who cleared forest for farms around Lake Llanquihue, and the architecture of nearby towns still has a distinctly German flavour. The park around Petrohue, Vicente Perez Rosales, is the oldest national park in Chile, established in 1926. Fuel is available in Puerto Varas and along the lake shore, but not at Petrohue, so fill up before the climb. Bring a jacket, since the lake air is cool, and allow time for the falls.
t.castro chile@-42.5,-73.8:
Castro is the capital of Chiloe, a green, rainy island off the coast of southern Chile that feels like a world apart, with its own food, mythology and architecture. Dalcahue, a smaller port on the island's east coast with a lively craft market, lies a short ride away.

The surface is generally good on the main road and rougher on side tracks, with the occasional pothole and plenty of damp patches. Fog and drizzle are common, and the weather can change in minutes, so waterproofs are a must. Summer, from December to March, is the driest season, but the island is rarely warm, and the light is soft and grey. Nature on Chiloe is soft and green, with temperate forests, tidal flats and misty hills. Dolphins and penguins live along the coast, and bird life is rich. The air smells of salt, wood smoke and wet grass.

Fill up the tank here, bring warm clothes and a good rain jacket, and keep your schedule flexible.
t.el bolson@-42.0,-71.5:
El Bolson lies in a sheltered valley on the eastern flank of the Andes, in the Rio Negro province of Argentina, and its reputation is of a green, relaxed mountain town with a hippie streak and a very good craft market. Traffic is light outside the summer holidays, and the best months for riding are November to April. In the 1970s, a wave of artists, craftspeople and back-to-the-landers settled here, drawn by the climate and the mountains, and the town declared itself a nuclear-free zone and a non-transgenic one. Nature is the real draw. The jagged peaks of the Andes rise above the town, with Cerro Piltriquitron standing out on the western side, and its slopes offer a forest of sculpted wooden figures. Lake Puelo, a short ride south, is a pristine glacier lake on the border with Chile, surrounded by forest. The air is crisp and smells of pine and wood smoke, and the rivers run cold and clear.

t.lago espejo@-40.7,-71.7:
Lago Espejo, the Mirror Lake, earns its name on still mornings, when the beech forest on the far shore and the snow on the peaks behind it are doubled in the water so perfectly that you lose the horizon. It lies about ten kilometres from Villa La Angostura, which is the nearest town of any size, and the place to buy fuel before setting out.

The road is the star. The Ruta de los Siete Lagos runs through the Nahuel Huapi and Lanin national parks for about a hundred kilometres, rising and dipping through forests of lenga, coihue and cypress, with a string of lakes appearing on either side and the peaks beyond. Tarmac is good, bends are long and flowing, and the road is wide enough to ride at an easy pace. Wind can gust across the lake shores, and rain and mist roll in quickly, sometimes with a chill that surprises you in summer. Traffic is heavy in January and February and on long weekends, so early mornings and late afternoons suit riders, as does the autumn, when the lenga forests turn red and gold. Winter brings snow and ice to the higher sections, and the road is sometimes closed or needs chains.

Today the lakes are a favourite for fishing, with trout and salmon introduced in the last century.

Nature is serene and varied. The forest smells of damp earth and resin, with ferns and bamboo thickets at the base of the trees, and the cry of the Magellanic woodpecker can be heard in the old beech. Condors sometimes soar above the peaks, and the water is cold, clear and an astonishing green or blue depending on the light. A pebbly beach on the lake makes a fine place to sit for a few minutes.

Fill up in Villa La Angostura, since fuel is scarce along the route. Bring a warm jacket and a camera, and take your time.
t.chacao@-41.8,-73.5:
Chacao is where the mainland ends and Chiloé begins, and the crossing is part of the pleasure. Ferries run back and forth across it all day from Pargua, carrying trucks, cars and motorcycles, and the trip takes about half an hour. On a clear day, you watch for dolphins and sea lions, and seabirds follow the boat, hoping for scraps.

Chiloé's wooden churches, sixteen of which are listed by UNESCO, were built by carpenters from shipbuilding traditions, using local cypress and larch and wooden pegs instead of nails. Their shingled towers and pastel colours are among the most distinctive sights in southern Chile. Ancud, the larger town, lies twenty-four kilometres to the south and has the fuel, supermarkets and a good fish market.

Chilote food is hearty and local, based on potatoes, seafood and above all curanto, a feast of shellfish, meat and potato cooked in a pit with hot stones. You can try it in the roadside restaurants, and a bowl of fish soup will warm you after a damp ferry crossing.

For riders, the island is a place of rolling green hills, small farms and sudden views of the sea, with Route 5 running down the middle. The roads are generally good, though there are potholes, and the traffic is light. Rain is frequent, and the climate is mild but wet, so waterproofs are essential, and fog can reduce visibility on the coast. Summer, from December to March, is the best season, though the weather is never reliable. Fuel is easy in the main towns, but less so in the villages, so top up when you can.
t.quellon@-43.1,-73.6:
Quellón sits at the southern end of Chiloé, a working port town of about twenty-two thousand people, where the road simply stops. This is the end of Route 5, the Chilean section of the Pan-American Highway, which runs more than three thousand kilometres from the northern desert to here, and a sign on the waterfront marks the spot. For anyone who has ridden down the long thin country, the moment of reaching it is oddly emotional, even if the town itself is practical rather than pretty.

The harbour is busy with fishing boats and salmon-farm vessels, and the smell of the sea and diesel hangs in the air. Salmon farming has become the main industry of the island, with pens in the sheltered waters of the channels, and it has brought work and controversy in about equal measure. A ferry runs from Quellón to Chaitén and Puerto Chacabuco on the mainland, linking Chiloé with the Carretera Austral. The town has fuel, supermarkets, a hospital and a selection of guesthouses and restaurants, so it is a good place to rest.

The cooking relies on a rich variety of local potatoes, of which there are said to be hundreds of varieties, and on smoked meat and rhubarb-like nalca stalks. The island's folk tradition is full of stories of sea creatures and spirits, and in a fishing town like this, they are told with a straight face.

South of town, the land becomes wilder, and the private Tantauco Park protects a large area of temperate rainforest and coast, with walking tracks and the chance to see foxes, pudú deer and rare birds. The road to it is gravel in places. Rain is normal in every month, so wear good waterproofs and expect fog. Summer is the best time for the ride, with longer days and a little more sun, though it is never really hot. Park the bike by the waterfront, and let the end of the road sink in.
t.pshaveli@42.1,45.3:
Pshaveli is not a place most people plan a trip around, which is part of its charm. It sits in Kakheti, Georgia's great wine province, where the broad flat valley of the Alazani river runs along the foot of the Greater Caucasus. From here, the mountains look like a wall: a long blue line of ridges, often with snow on top, that marks the border with Dagestan and Chechnya and shuts out half the sky to the north. The nearest towns are Akhmeta, a small and workmanlike place a few kilometres off, and Telavi, the regional capital, about twenty kilometres away.

For the ride, this is the point where the lowlands end and the real climb begins. The surface is the usual Georgian mix: some good tar, some patches that suddenly turn to potholes, and the occasional cow standing in the road as if to remind you who owns it. Villages are strung along the way with fruit trees, walnut groves, vines trained over wooden frames and houses with carved balconies. Dogs, chickens and the occasional tractor demand your attention more than any traffic does.

Kakheti is where Georgian winemaking is said to date back thousands of years, and the traditional method still survives here: grapes pressed and fermented with their skins in a buried clay vessel called a qvevri. Amber wines, cloudy and tannic, are the local pride, and even a small village can have a family cellar that will pour you a glass if you stop and look curious. If you are riding, one polite sip is the only sensible measure; the mountain road ahead is not forgiving.

Think of this stop as the last proper preparation. Fuel is easiest in Akhmeta or Telavi, and you should leave here with a full tank, because the road beyond heads up into Tusheti, where no pump awaits. Take water, a warm layer, a rain jacket and some cash in lari. The morning is the time to move: clouds tend to build over the Caucasus by afternoon, and the high roads are better crossed in clear light. Pause, look up at the ridge, and decide whether you are really ready for what comes after the last village.
t.abano pass@42.1,45.5:
This is the road that gives Georgia its reputation for dramatic riding. The Abano Pass, at a little over 2,800 metres, is the only vehicle route into Tusheti, a remote highland region of the Greater Caucasus, and it is a rough, narrow track that clings to mountainsides, crosses streams and passes within a short skid of some long drops. It is not paved. It is not wide. In places two vehicles meeting is a matter of negotiation, and the sign of a good day is making it over the top without a puncture.

The climb from the Kakheti side starts in forest and quickly leaves it behind, rising through beech and birch to alpine meadow and bare rock. The surface is loose stone, ruts and in a few places running water, and the corners are tight hairpins with a very real edge. Ride in the dry, stand on the pegs where you can, and take your time. Local drivers in old Delicas and Mitsubishis do this road daily, often faster than is wise, so keep right and be ready to stop on a blind bend. It is typically open from around June through October; snow closes it for the rest of the year, and storms can shut it earlier.

At the top, the world opens in every direction. Peaks stack up behind peaks, the temperature drops sharply, and there is often a wind that tries to take your lid off. Cloud can pour over the ridge in minutes, so keep an eye on the sky and do not linger if it turns black. The meadows are full of wildflowers in early summer, and the shepherds who bring flocks over this pass each year, a tradition that has gone on for generations, may wave from the slope.

Start with a full tank, carry some spare water and food, and tell someone your plan. Phone signal comes and goes. This is a serious road, not a casual stop, and it repays patience with one of the great mountain views in the Caucasus. Respect it and it will be the day you talk about for years.
t.omalo@42.4,45.6:
After the Abano Pass, Omalo feels like a reward you did not quite believe in. It is the main village of Tusheti, a high, remote valley system in the northeast of Georgia, on the far side of the Caucasus watershed, and it is split into two parts: Upper Omalo on the hilltop, Lower Omalo a little below. For centuries the Tush people drove their sheep over the pass each autumn to winter in the lowlands, and returned each summer. The tradition is still alive, and this is a landscape of stone towers, slate roofs, dry-stone walls and sheep as far as the eye can see.

Above Upper Omalo stands the fortress of Keselo, a cluster of old stone towers and houses built for defence in a region where mountain clans had plenty of reasons to fear raiders. Walking up there takes only a short time, and the view down the valley, with the Alazani headwaters and the ridge of the Caucasus behind, is worth the effort. Further up the valleys are villages such as Dartlo, with its tight cluster of towers, and the wider Tusheti National Park protects forests, meadows and alpine ground rich with flowers and rare birds.

Food is the thing you will remember. Tusheti has its own cheese, a smoky, salty sheep's cheese often called guda, and its own dumplings, called khinkali in the Georgian style but sometimes made a little differently here. Guesthouses serve big, simple meals of potatoes, bread, soup, local lamb and homemade chacha or beer if you are not riding. A night here is far better than a quick passing visit, because the light on the towers at dusk and the cold clear sky at night are part of the story.

The practical side demands respect. There is no reliable fuel in the area, so you must arrive with enough to get back over the pass. Roads in the valley are gravel and rock, and the season is short, roughly early summer to early autumn, dictated by the snow on Abano. Bring warm clothing even in July, cash in lari, and spare tubes. Cell coverage is patchy. The nearest real towns on the other side are Akhmeta and Telavi, a long, slow day away.
t.gombori pass@41.8,45.2:
The Gombori Pass is the doorway between two Georgias. On one side lies the dry, open country of the Iori valley and the capital's hinterland; on the other, beyond the ridge, the lush Alazani valley that is the heart of Kakheti wine country. The road crosses the Gombori range at roughly 1,600 metres, climbing through thick oak and beech forest in tightly packed bends, and for the rider it is a short, sweet change of scene: cool shade, damp leaves, and a drop into a different climate on the other side.

The corners come in tidy sequences, mostly medium-radius with a few hairpins, and the surface is usually serviceable though prone to patches, loose gravel at the apex, and the occasional cow. Fog is common. Cloud banks up against the ridge from the west, and it is entirely possible to ride up in thick mist and come down into bright sun, or the reverse. Trucks use the pass too, so expect to slow behind a diesel cloud on the climbs. Stay out of the middle of the bends when visibility drops, and avoid riding it in heavy rain after dark.

Wine is the story. The Gombori crossing is the usual route for Tbilisi families heading to Kakheti for harvest time in autumn, when roadside stalls sell churchkhela, the walnut-and-grape-juice candy that hangs in strings like candles, and jugs of new wine. The area around Telavi, Tsinandali and Sighnaghi has a wine tradition thousands of years deep, and the old method of fermenting grapes in buried clay qvevri is a point of national pride. The forest here is also home to wild boar and a good number of birds, though you are far more likely to see sheep.

The best bet for fuel is Sagarejo, on the western approach, or Telavi on the east. The pass is open all year in principle, but winter can bring ice and snow, so it is best between late spring and autumn. Early morning gives the clearest air, and the late afternoon light as you descend toward Kakheti, with the Caucasus lined up across the valley, is superb.
t.telavi@41.9,45.5:
Telavi is the capital of Kakheti, a town of about twenty-two thousand people that serves as the regional hub for wine, farming and old-fashioned Georgian hospitality. It sits on the northwest side of the Alazani valley, with the Tsiv-Gombori range behind and, on a clear day, the white wall of the Greater Caucasus ahead across the plain. It is a good place to stop, with real shops and a real market, and with enough history to keep you interested between mouthfuls.

For centuries this was the seat of the Kakhetian kings, and the town's most famous ruler was Erekle II, who in the eighteenth century united Kakheti with neighbouring Kartli and then, under growing pressure from Persia, turned to Russia for protection. His palace, Batonis Tsikhe, still stands in the old town, and a large statue of him on horseback looks over the main square. A short walk away is a huge plane tree said to be around nine hundred years old, with a trunk wide enough that people shelter inside the hollow. It is not hard to find, and it is more impressive than it sounds.

The riding around Telavi is gentler than in the mountains. The plain is a patchwork of vineyards, orchards and maize, the roads are straight and usually in decent shape, and the pace is relaxed. Watch out for tractors, horse carts and the odd flock crossing, and treat any road on market day with respect. Nearby are the wine estates of Tsinandali, where the Chavchavadze family hosted poets and nobles in the nineteenth century, and the fortified church complex at Gremi, a former royal town.

As a rest stop, Telavi is excellent. Fuel is easy to find, there are plenty of cafes serving mtsvadi, the grilled pork skewers that every Georgian cook argues about, plus fresh bread from a tone, the clay oven, and several wine bars and cellars if you are staying the night. Guesthouses are cheap and friendly. If you are coming off the Gombori ridge or heading up toward the Caucasus passes, this is where you gather yourself, eat well and refill the tank for the next section.
t.route of the seven lakes point 2@-40.5,-:
Somewhere on this part of the road you cross from the valley of San Martin into the lake district proper, and the first of the lakes appears among dark forest. The seven lakes along the route are glacial, scooped out by ice during the last ice age and filled with meltwater, and each has its own colour, from steel blue to green to a milky turquoise when the light is right. Machonico, Falkner and Villarino are among those you pass, and they line up like beads along the road.

Fill the tank before leaving San Martin and bring something to eat, because there are only a few small kiosks and campsites in the forest. Those places open in summer, and their hours are unpredictable.

The riding is among the best in Argentine Patagonia. The road weaves through the forest in long, smooth bends, sometimes climbing, sometimes dipping to a lakeshore. Most of it is paved and in good condition now, though a few gravel sections remained until recently, and it makes sense to check the current state. Look out for cattle and for sudden patches of damp under the trees. In the early morning, mist hangs over the water and the forest smells of moist earth and cinnamon-scented bark.

This is also protected land, and much of the road passes through Lanin and Nahuel Huapi national parks. The forest holds southern beech, the strange monkey puzzle tree on some slopes, and cypress, and in the lakes there are trout, brought in by early settlers and now a big draw for fly fishermen. Condors circle above the higher ridges, and you may see a fox cross the road at dusk. Stop at the signed viewpoints to take photographs, since the road itself has few places to pull over safely. A thin jacket will not do here; the temperature can fall quickly.

t.frutillar@-41.1,-73.1:
Frutillar looks as if a piece of Bavaria had been dropped on the shore of a Chilean lake, and in a way it was. German settlers arrived in southern Chile in the mid nineteenth century, invited by the government to colonise the forested south, and they built wooden houses with steep roofs and neat gardens on the western shore of Lago Llanquihue. Their descendants still run bakeries that sell kuchen, the cakes made with berries and cream, and the town keeps a quiet, tidy air.

The lake is enormous, the second largest in Chile, with a surface that stretches to the horizon and a backdrop of volcanoes. Across the water, the cone of Osorno rises in a nearly perfect shape, capped with snow, while Calbuco, rougher and more menacing, stands to the right. On a clear day the view is superb, and the lakeside promenade is the best place to take it in. The theatre on the shore, built in modern times, hosts classical music events and has become a major cultural venue in the region, a surprising presence in a small town.

The ride along the lake is a pleasure. The road follows the shoreline from Puerto Varas through farmland and small settlements, with views opening and closing as the road dips and rises. It is generally smooth, with gentle bends, and traffic can be heavy on summer weekends. Cyclists are common, and so are tractors and trucks hauling milk and timber. The weather is changeable, with wind off the lake and showers that pass in minutes, so a light rain jacket is useful.

Frutillar has a few shops and cafes but no big supermarkets; Puerto Varas, about twenty kilometres away, has more choice if you need to stock up. The German heritage shows in the German museum, with a reconstructed settler's house, mill and water-powered machines in a park above the town, and gives a clear picture of how the colonists lived.

Try the kuchen, particularly in the afternoon, when it is served with strong coffee. Sit outside if the weather allows, and watch Osorno change colour as the light shifts.
